title: Give up pride, holy ones
hookLine: saadho man kaa maan tiaago: holy ones, give up the mind's pride (Gauri M9, ang 219)
tomorrow: The world as a wall of sand

cards: Someone corrects you in front of other people, even about something tiny, the spelling of a name, the year a film came out. Watch what happens inside. A flash of heat.

A quick story about why you were actually right, or why it doesn't matter, or why they're being annoying. It takes about half a second. That flash is pride, and it guards the mind like a bouncer at a door.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Raag Gauri begins by speaking straight to the people who think they're past all that.

teach.h: MAN KAA MAAN: THE MIND'S PRIDE.
teach.b: The hymn opens saadho man kaa maan tiaago.
Holy ones, give up the mind's pride. Man is the mind, and maan is pride, honor, self-regard. Man kaa maan: the two words nearly rhyme, as if pride were the mind's shadow, following it everywhere.
And notice who he's talking to: saadho, holy ones, the good and devout. Pride can grow quietly in good people, because they have real things to be proud of. In paraphrase, the hymn goes on.
Run day and night from lust, from anger, and from bad company.

The one who knows pleasure and pain as the same, and honor and dishonor too, who stays beyond joy and grief, has understood the essence of the world. Leave both praise and blame, and seek the state of freedom.
Then the last line, in paraphrase: this is a hard game, says Nanak; only a few, turned toward the Guru, understand it. An honest ending. He doesn't pretend it's easy.

teach.h: A HARD GAME, PLAYED ROUND BY ROUND.
teach.b: Giving up pride is less a single decision than a game you keep playing, round after round, every time the flash of heat comes.
And here's the turn: pride and honor are the same word, maan. The pride he asks you to drop is the need to be honored. Let that go, and dishonor loses its sting.
Someone corrects you, and it's just information. That's the freedom the hymn points at.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabad 'saadho man kaa maan tiaago' in Raag Gauri in kirtan, and many hear it as a reminder that pride is the danger of the devout.

o: pride, the mind's need to be honored
the mind itself, the thinking self
a vow made to the Guru in trouble

games.q: give up pride — tap the pairs.

s: the hymn is spoken to wrongdoers who need to repent
it's spoken to saadho, the holy ones; pride can grow quietly in good people.
the hymn calls giving up pride easy once you decide
it calls it a hard game that only a few understand.
in the hymn, maan means both pride and honor
drop the need to be honored, and dishonor loses its sting.

games.q: you're one of the devout, and you've done a lot of good. who is the hymn's first line spoken to?
o: the people who have done wrong.
the holy ones, people like you.
games.why: saadho man kaa maan tiaago: holy ones, give up the mind's pride. the warning is for the good, who have real things to be proud of.

practice: Let the mind wander, and watch for a thought that puffs you up: I'm better at this than them, they should have asked me, I deserve more credit.
When one comes, don't argue with it; name it, pride, and set it down the way you'd put down a heavy bag. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Maan, the mind's pride, the need to be honored. Guru Tegh Bahadur tells even the holy ones to let go of it. He calls it a hard game.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: maan, pride or honor. In the hymn it sits right beside man, the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: give up the pride. Each flash of heat is one more round of the hard game. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Raag Gauri, Mahalla 9, 'saadho man kaa maan tiaago' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 219)
